oil.summary: Crude markets posted a split session on 24 November, with WTI recovering 1.90% to $81.69/bbl while Brent slipped 0.97% to $88.50/bbl — the divergence likely reflecting distinct quality and regional flow dynamics. The backdrop remains deeply bearish on a monthly basis, with both benchmarks down roughly 20-24% over the past month. Strait of Hormuz tension stayed elevated after Iran claimed three tankers struck mines and Bahrain reported an Iranian strike on an industrial site, yet prices struggled to sustain a risk premium as the US naval blockade tightens Iran's oil revenues. OPEC+ fractures are adding to the bearish undertow: Iraq is openly contesting OPEC+'s capacity assessment, Saudi Arabia revised its GDP contraction to 2.1% (from 3.6%) as more oil reaches market, and options markets price a 77% chance of a production cut at the May 2027 meeting. The Russia diesel deal and sanctions relief discussions add further complexity to supply-side optics.
drivers: Strait of Hormuz incidents (tanker mine strikes, Bahrain strike report) provide a geopolitical floor but insufficient to offset supply-side bearishness
OPEC+ cohesion under pressure as Iraq disputes its production capacity ceiling, raising compliance doubts ahead of the May meeting
US blockade squeezing Iranian oil revenues while Russia-US oil deal diplomacy muddies the sanctions landscape

gas.summary: Henry Hub surged 15.26% on the day to $3.67/MMBtu, extending a remarkable monthly gain of 41.05% — the standout price move across all energy sectors today. No specific US-side headline was provided to explain today's spike, so the driver set is likely a combination of early-winter demand pull and position squaring; the data provided is thin on US-specific catalysts. In Europe, TTF edged up 0.75% to €90.405/MWh, its fourth consecutive session of gains, as an incoming cold snap is accelerating storage withdrawals from already-depleted reserves. The year-on-year context is stark: European gas prices are reportedly up 163% over the past twelve months. The EU's advancing legislation to ban Russian gas imports adds a structural tightening signal, while Iran's worsening domestic gas shortage — driven by war-related infrastructure damage — removes a potential alternative supply source from the regional picture.
drivers: European cold snap driving accelerated storage withdrawals from depleted inventories, pushing TTF to a fourth consecutive daily gain
Henry Hub +15% single-day spike on strong winter demand signals; underlying US catalyst data is limited in today's feed
EU legislation to ban Russian gas imports and Iran's domestic gas infrastructure damage both point to tighter medium-term supply globally

power.summary: EU carbon (EUA) fell 1.05% to $79.025/EUA, extending a 4.94% weekly decline and a 6.07% monthly retreat. The softness in EUAs sits in contrast to rising TTF gas prices, which typically support carbon demand as gas-fired generation becomes more expensive and marginal abatement costs shift. Headlines on the power and carbon desk are thin today; the most relevant contextual items are the EU's 22nd Russia sanctions package — raising questions about how much further the bloc's sanctions toolbox can reach — and a Central Asian pilot project for a regional electricity market, which is early-stage and unlikely to move near-term European prices. No power price data was provided for European day-ahead markets, limiting the analytical picture.
drivers: EUA prices sliding despite rising TTF, suggesting demand-side weakness or profit-taking is outweighing fuel-switching carbon pressure
EU's 22nd Russia sanctions package signals continued policy tightening but its incremental energy market impact appears limited at this stage
Power sector news flow is sparse today; Central Asia regional grid pilot is too nascent to influence near-term market dynamics
